cinematic_inference.protagonist_occupation: Conservator / Collections Manager at a regional museum
cinematic_inference.body_design: 5'6" (168 cm), medium build with lean musculature from lifting crates and working long hours standing; pronounced, capable hands with short, practical nails and a faint pale scar along the pad of the right index finger; neutral posture that tightens when stressed; skin olive-toned with subtle sun freckles across the nose and forearms.
cinematic_inference.ethnicity_design: Colombian-American (Latina), bicultural presence that informs quiet confidence and community ties without defining the profession.
cinematic_inference.hair_design: Dark brown, naturally wavy, shoulder-length usually worn in a low, slightly messy bun for studio work or loose with a middle part for public appearances; a few silvering strands at the temples but overall thick and serviceable.
cinematic_inference.wardrobe_design: Smart-casual practical wardrobe: soft, neutral linen and cotton button shirts; slim, tapered chinos or dark denim; lightweight tweed or utility jacket for gallery visits; comfortable leather ankle boots with non-slip soles; archival-smock lab coat or sleeveless canvas conservation apron for studio scenes; muted, minimal jewelry (thin gold band and small stud earrings); always carries a worn canvas messenger bag containing gloves, field notebook, cotton swabs, and a compact loupe.
cinematic_inference.casting_rationale: A conservator/collections manager fits the profile by combining meticulous, tactile work with interpersonal responsibilities, creating opportunities for quiet intensity and pressured moments. The role supports a grounded, community-oriented cultural tone and a methodical work style while offering strong visual motifs—tools, light, crates—that reveal inner steadiness and controlled anxiety under stress.

stable_identity: Temperament: introspective, steadfast, slightly anxious under stress
Economic: financially independent or partly independent
Interpersonal style: reserved, warm with close contacts
director_profile.social_dynamics: Reserved in larger staff meetings and public events, she is deferential but assertive when collections' integrity is at stake; has a small circle of trusted colleagues (a practical registrar, an idealistic curator, a sympathetic preparator) and routinely negotiates with contractors, donors, and volunteer docents. She mentors interns quietly and becomes quietly protective over objects and people she trusts.
director_profile.professional_vibe: Hands-on specialist who balances meticulous studio treatment with logistics and small-scale diplomacy—methodical in procedure, meticulous with documentation, and pragmatic about budgets and timelines.
director_profile.visual_vibe: Muted, tactile color palette (stone grays, warm olives, indigo) with close-up, object-focused cinematography: gloved hands, magnified surface textures, directional examination lamps, stacked archival crates, and narrow vault corridors that emphasize intimate scale and quiet intensity.

director_profile.parallel_story_rule: Do not recast the employer as a private religious or family institution; the job remains a museum-based conservator/collections manager and any personal faith or family life belongs to off-duty identity, not the workplace.

occupation_selection.job_title: Conservator / Collections Manager at a regional museum
occupation_selection.rationale: A conservator/collections manager balances methodical, detail-focused work with occasional high-stakes, human-facing moments—ideal for a reserved, introspective woman who is steadfast and slightly anxious under stress. The day-to-day allows for focused, tactile labor (cleaning, stabilizing, photographing artifacts) that suits a methodical temperament and offers concrete visual interest: studio benches, microscopes, archival crates, examination lights, and hands-in-gloves close-ups. The role also supports varied scenes and relationships—collaborating with curators and installers, coordinating with registrars and registrants, overseeing condition reports and crate movements, doing site visits for loans or conservation treatments, and giving occasional gallery talks or donor walkthroughs. Those elements create dynamic, changing environments (studio, storage vaults, galleries, loading docks, field locations) without relying mainly on paperwork or meetings, and plausibly support financial independence through museum salary or contract work. Casting a conservator avoids obvious occupational tropes while offering a visually rich, credible world for character-driven storytelling.
